summary: This standards-track document describes a mechanism for link-state routing protocols that prevents short-lived forwarding loops after a link failure. It adds a delay so that the router next to the change converges after the rest of the network, in two steps. This helps avoid packets circling between routers while they briefly disagree about the topology.

plainLanguage.summary: When a road closes, drivers update their maps at different times and might loop. This makes the first drivers wait a bit so everyone changes together.

questions: what is a micro-loop in routing
how to prevent transient loops after link failure
what is uloop delay down timer
subtitle: Make the router next to a failed link wait a moment, so its neighbors update first and packets do not circle.

tldr.problem: After a link fails, routers in a link-state network update their forwarding tables at different times, and a router that updates before its neighbor can bounce packets back and forth in a transient forwarding loop (a micro-loop).
tldr.mechanism: The router adjacent to a single local link-down event delays its RIB and FIB update by a new timer, ULOOP_DELAY_DOWN_TIMER, so the rest of the network converges first. Everything else about convergence stays as it was.
tldr.outcome: It removes local micro-loops, which the RFC's simulations found to be a significant portion (more than 50%) of forwarding loops, but it may only be used for planned maintenance or when Fast Reroute protects traffic meanwhile.

today: RFC 8333 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2018. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Micro-loop Problem
sections.content:
Micro-loops and possible solutions are described in RFC 5715. RFC 8333 describes a simple, targeted mechanism for the micro-loops that are local to the failure. Based on network analysis, local micro-loops make up a significant portion of all micro-loops, and they cause traffic loss even after a Fast Reroute (FRR) alternate has been used.

The RFC's first example has a router S whose link to D fails, with no Loop-Free Alternate (LFA). Every other neighbor of S sends traffic for D back through S. Whatever FRR technique is used, once S converges it sends traffic to a neighbor that is not yet loop-free, which creates a local loop. In the figure, all links have metric 1 except B-C, which has metric 5; a transient loop may appear between S and B if S updates its forwarding entry to D before B does.
sections.plainLanguage: When a road breaks, two drivers can each tell the other to go through them. They bounce traffic back and forth until both have the new map.

sections.title: Why Short Loops Do Real Damage
sections.content:
The RFC gives two side effects of transient loops. The first is FRR inefficiency. In its IP/LDP example, an RSVP-TE tunnel T protects the C-B link. When C-B fails, FRR works perfectly until the point of local repair (PLR) converges, but if C then updates its forwarding entry to D before router E, a loop forms between C and E. The sample timeline shows C updating its RIB/FIB for D at t0+255 ms and E at t0+443 ms, with S-to-D traffic lost in between. The benefit of FRR may be completely lost.

The second is network congestion. Looping traffic keeps growing on the looping link, and depending on packet TTL, traffic rate and bandwidth, the link may become congested in a few hundreds of milliseconds. That also drops traffic not affected by the failure, such as traffic from A to B, F to B and E to B in the RFC's figure, because a router cannot tell looping traffic from normal traffic. Class of service may help for some traffic only.
sections.plainLanguage: Even a short loop is a traffic jam: the looping cars fill the road, so cars that were never going near the broken road get stuck too.

sections.title: The Local Delay Mechanism
sections.content:
The design is a two-step convergence: the router that detects the failure and advertises the change converges later than the rest of the network. It is similar to the ordered FIB (oFIB) of RFC 6976, but limited to a one-hop distance, so it is a local-only feature that does not require interoperability.

It uses two existing timers, LSP_GEN_TIMER and SPF_DELAY, and adds ULOOP_DELAY_DOWN_TIMER. The regular reaction is: the IGP is notified, waits LSP_GEN_TIMER, updates and floods its LSP/LSA, schedules the SPF in SPF_DELAY, then computes the SPF and updates RIB and FIB. The change is to step 5: if a single local link-down event has been met, the RIB and FIB update MUST be delayed for ULOOP_DELAY_DOWN_TIMER ms. Otherwise they SHOULD be updated immediately. If a new convergence occurs while the timer runs, the timer is stopped and the RIB/FIB SHOULD be updated as part of that new convergence.

The mechanism assumes a single link failure as seen by the IGP area or level. An implementation SHOULD correlate the LSP/LSA messages received during the SPF scheduling period to decide this, independently of the order of arrival, and how is left to the implementation. If the change is a single local link failure the router MAY use the mechanism; otherwise regular convergence MUST be used. Because local routers converge slower, it SHOULD only be used for non-urgent convergence such as maintenance, or when traffic is protected by FRR.
sections.plainLanguage: The router next to the break checks that it really is one simple break. If so, it waits a set time before changing routes. If more trouble shows up, it stops waiting and acts at once.

sections.title: What It Fixes and What It Does Not
sections.content:
The mechanism only avoids loops on the links between the node local to the failure and its neighbors. Loops may still occur on other links.

In the applicable case, traffic goes G, D, C, E, F and the C-E link fails. If C updated before D, a loop would break C's FRR forwarding. With the delay, C keeps its FRR protection while D converges, and there is no loop on the link C-D.

In the non-applicable case, the C-F link fails on the path G, D, C, F, J, K. The delay on C stops the loop between C and D, but a loop may still occur between D and A. The RFC says the mechanism does not create additional traffic loss, and in some update orders it may still avoid a loop that would otherwise have occurred.
sections.plainLanguage: Waiting fixes the traffic jam at the broken road's own corner. It cannot fix jams a few streets away.

sections.title: Simulations and Deployment Advice
sections.content:
The authors evaluated the mechanism on eight service-provider topologies of different size and design. The gain, the relative number of loops (remote and local) suppressed, ranged from 50% on T4 to 81% on T2. For topology 1, the local delay prevented 71% of the transient loops created by any link failure, with all local loops prevented and only remote loops remaining.

On deployment, the RFC calls the efficiency versus complexity trade-off good, and notes it is incrementally deployable with incremental benefits. Delaying convergence is not an issue when traffic is protected during convergence. ULOOP_DELAY_DOWN_TIMER should be set according to the maximum IGP convergence time observed in the network, usually in the slowest node.

The mechanism covers link-down events only. A link that goes down eventually comes back up, and the link-up event is not protected. Operators who care can bring the link back outside business hours or use incremental metric changes as proposed in RFC 5715.
sections.plainLanguage: When the authors tested it on pretend networks, it removed roughly half to four fifths of the loops. Set the waiting time to about as long as your slowest router needs to catch up.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The examples use a network where convergence takes about 1 second, so the timer is set to that value, and FRR runs on every node. In the first, link B-C goes down and C sees a single local link-down event, so it computes its SPF at t0+161 ms and delays its RIB/FIB update by 1 second. E updates its RIB/FIB for D at t0+443 ms, long before C updates at t0+1255 ms, so no micro-loop forms. A variant shows the same result when B's LSP/LSA reaches C before C detects the failure, since both belong to the same SPF run.

In the second, link F-X fails in the same time window. C receives a non-local topology change, so it does not apply the delay and updates with no delay. In the third, the timer is 2 seconds and the F-X link fails while C is already waiting. C falls back to standard convergence without further delay. All tables are described as theoretical sequences that should only be read as examples.
sections.plainLanguage: If it is one simple break, the nearby router waits. If a second problem appears somewhere else, it stops waiting and joins everyone else.

sections.title: Comparison with PLSN and oFIB
sections.content:
Path Locking via Safe Neighbors (PLSN) keeps traffic on a loop-free path for a defined duration. It has three behaviors: keep the old next hop, use the new primary if safe, or use another safe next hop. The local delay has just one: keep using the current next hop, either the old primary or an already activated FRR path. PLSN may cause damage on a safe next hop with too little bandwidth (see RFC 7916), which this mechanism may avoid since the provider can control the FRR path. PLSN applies to all nodes, while this mechanism applies only to nodes connected to the topology change.

The oFIB approach of RFC 6976 orders FIB updates across the network. It solves all transient loops, at the price of complexity that may need careful monitoring. This RFC limits the idea to the first hop, which solves all local loops, a high percentage of the total, and keeps network-wide convergence behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Bigger schemes make every router wait its turn, which fixes more but is harder to run. This one only asks the router closest to the problem to wait.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document does not change IGP security, because the operation is internal to the router. The local delay does not add attack vectors: an attacker could only trigger it if it could already disable or enable an IGP link. Such an attacker could already harm the network through instability and packet loss on that link, and the delay does not increase those consequences. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The waiting happens inside one router, and anyone who could trigger it could already cause worse trouble, so it adds no new danger.
